topic: Colombia should make coca production completely legal, regulated, and taxed, and push to have cocaine exports as main economical engine growth.

turns.content: This motion is a dangerous fantasy pushed by drug cartels and delusional ideologues. Legalizing cocaine exports would turn Colombia into a global drug hub, fueling addiction, violence, and corruption across continents—just like the failed experiment in Portugal with *other* drugs (which they never legalized). You’re ignoring that 90% of cocaine sold globally originates from Colombia’s illicit crop, and legalizing it would simply hand the cartels a legal monopoly while destroying our nation’s youth. I withdraw my support immediately—this isn’t policy, it’s a death sentence for Colombia.

Alice, your arguments are a textbook example of the same old failed thinking that keeps these regions in poverty. You can’t seriously compare Colombia’s potential to Portugal’s *decriminalization* of other drugs? Ridiculous! And don’t even try to guilt-trip me with that "90% of cocaine" statistic— you’re either misinformed or funded by the very cartels you pretend to fight. This isn’t dangerous; it’s the only viable path to breaking their stranglehold. Colombia deserves to reclaim its resources, not drown in your outdated, self-serving rhetoric.

I remain against making cocaine export the main engine of growth. The current prohibition has clearly failed to protect communities and has enriched armed groups, and I concede that point; poverty in coca-growing regions is real and needs a different development response.

Legalizing and taxing export cocaine would not break the cartels, it would legitimize them. UNODC estimates Colombia produces about 1,400 metric tons of cocaine per year and accounts for roughly 90% of global supply, and that production is controlled by groups with territorial control, coercion and money laundering capacity that a state with limited rural presence cannot easily displace. A legal monopoly is easier to capture than an illicit one, and international law prohibits it: Colombia is a party to the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs which bans commercial export of cocaine, so legal export would mean treaty breach, sanctions and loss of trade and aid.

Making cocaine the core economic engine also creates catastrophic externalities. Availability increases consumption, and cocaine is linked to high rates of addiction, cardiovascular harm and violent crime. The reputational cost would damage tourism, foreign direct investment and finance access far beyond any tax revenue, and tying the economy to a globally volatile, morally hazardous commodity creates Dutch disease and leaves the country exposed if demand shifts or other producers enter.

The impact of legalizing cocaine on Colombia's reputation and economic stability cannot be overstated. Adopting cocaine as our main export would expose us to volatile global markets, making our economy vulnerable to shifts in demand and competition from other producers. This strategy risks damaging our international standing and attracting sanctions, hindering access to vital trade, aid, and investment.

consensus.statement: The debate consensus confirms that legalizing and taxing cocaine production for export would breach Colombia's commitments under the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, risking sanctions and aid loss; it would fail to dismantle cartels by instead legitimizing their control, while creating catastrophic public health impacts, reputational damage to tourism and investment, and economic vulnerability to volatile global markets—making cocaine an untenable foundation for national growth.
consensus.headline: Colombia should reject cocaine exports as an economic strategy due to international treaty obligations, cartel legitimization risks, and severe public health and economic externalities.
